messages.body_plain:
Hi Gianluca,

Will wait for maybe Chris to confirm this -- but it seems that a ctmm object was created assuming that all data belongs to the same animal/id. Your data does not seem to have an Id column- There maybe duplicated timestamps.
I always have trouble removing duplicates through R due to differences in minutes and seconds -- so I do it in excel.  And I create separate ctmm objects for each individual by separating the data for each individual from the move object dataframe.

I was able to create a ctmm object using your code

Hope this helps.

messages.subject: Re: path reconstruction
messages.subject_clean: path reconstruction
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,
Thanks so much for your very quick reply.

Ah...so am I understanding correctly that the following would give me the radius in x and y of the 95% confidence ellipse for a point?

sqrt(qchisq(0.95, df=2)) * sqrt(COV.x.x)
sqrt(qchisq(0.95, df=2)) * sqrt(COV.y.y)

If so, I have values that make sense!

Thanks again,
Jenny

On Tuesday, April 28, 2020 at 10:18:44 PM UTC-4, Christen Fleming wrote:
> Hi Jenny,
>
> 1.) Looks good.
>
> 2.1) After what you've done (error calibration & movement model selection) you run the selected movement model and calibrated tracking data through predict(). The output will have both location point estimates and error ellipses in the columns of the dataframe.
>
> 2.2) That sounds reasonable to me. For coverage you might try looking at the standardized prediction errors. I.e., if
>
> d <- predicted_location - triangulated_location
> S <- predicted_COV + triangulated_COV
>
> then (d %*% solve(S) %*% d) should be (approximately) chi^2 with two degrees of freedom. But as far as how fast the error ellipse will expand out, that will be dictated by the tau values.
>
> 2.3) simulate does not give estimates, but randomly sampled trajectories that are consistent with the model and data. predict's point estimate should be closer to the truth than most realizations from simulate. predict output should have variance/covariance columns corresponding to the point estimates (COV.xx, COV.yy, COV.xy, or VAR.xy). You don't choose between simulate and predict based on accuracy, but based on use case.
>
> 3) I recommend saving objects that take a long time to compute to an R data file via save().
>
> Best,
> Chris
>
> On Tuesday, April 28, 2020 at 5:17:47 PM UTC-4, Jenny Smetzer wrote:
> >
> > Hi Chris,
> >
> >
> > I have automated telemetry data collected on a few hundred birds, with a typical (but gappy) sampling rate of 2 to 4 minutes. I used tags at known locations to develop models that predict error for each detection based on covariates. I have a few things that I want to do with these data in ctmm, and would like to make sure I am using the package correctly.
> >
> >
> > 1) Incorporating error: Since we already had an error estimate for each point (in meters), I named this column “VAR.xy” in my data, made sure this column was included in my telemetry object, and incorporated into models like so, where my_stack is my data formatted as a move stack:
> >
> >
> > yourAnimals <- as.telemetry(my_stack, keep = c('VAR.xy'))
> >
> > GUESS <- ctmm.guess(yourAnimals[[1]], CTMM = ctmm(error=TRUE), interactive=FALSE)
> >
> > FIT <- ctmm.select(yourAnimals[[1]], GUESS,  trace = T,  verbose = T)
> >
> >
> > I would like to confirm that I am doing this correctly in ctmm, since my data do not have the same structure as the Argos data in the examples.
> >
> >
> > 2) Probabilistic path reconstruction: Some of the birds’ tracks have greater error (up to ~ 350 m), and are sparser with some gaps varying from a few hours to a few days. We want to use these data to explore exposure to avian malaria, so it would be very helpful to predict over some of the short time gaps, or at least improve our existing location estimates for these birds. The location estimates are based on triangulation, and are thus “blind” to estimates at nearby times.
> >
> >
> > 2.1)   Do I understand correctly that with Kriging we may be able to predict location at the observed times with a bit more precision, as we can leverage the auto-correlation structure of the data? If so, how can we estimate this precision? An error ellipse for each location estimate would be ideal.
> >
> >
> > 2.2) To explore how far we can reasonably interpolate into time gaps I have thinned the points on a fairly high-resolution individual (median lag of 4 mins) to make artificial gaps of varying duration. To assess the spatial accuracy of predicted location I compared predicted (and simulated) locations to the “true” locations that were thinned. Is this approach a defensible way of figuring out how far out into a gap it might be reasonable to predict (or simulate)? I assume the determination for this bird is not necessarily relevant for the ~ 250 others? Is there a better way to determine a reasonable dt.max argument, perhaps based on the tau estimate?
> >
> >
> > 2.3) The predict function (based on the best OU error model) is giving point estimates far closer to the actual thinned locations than the simulate function. For instance, with my fake 12 minute gaps I am getting point estimates 143 (±114m) from the “true” path, and the simulate function is giving me point estimates 228 (±161m) from the “true” path. Considering the mean error for this individual is ~ 140m neither of these seems too terrible, and I figured interpolating with dt.max of 12 mins is OK. Since the predict function is returning better point estimates I am inclined to use this. However, it would be nice to also have some measure of confidence at both the observed and interpolated points, and I am not sure I can get this with predict…perhaps I need to use a lot of simulated tracks?
> >
> >
> > 3) I noticed that the FAQ mentions not to save the workspace. This feels like a dumb R question, but....what then is the recommended method to save model results? I have automated R to output the model summary, and the AKDE raster and shapefiles for each individual, but then found myself wanting to go back and do something else with the model output later and had to re-run. I am probably missing something obvious.
> >
> >
> > Thank you for any insight. It is exciting to learn how to use this package!
> >
> > Best,
> >
> > Jenny
> >
> >

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I'm working on putting together a model that explores the effect of a number of spatial covariates (distance to water, density of households, etc.) on where birds like to hang out. I started out with a count model and summed relocations within grid cells covering the area of interest and put together a poisson model to explore count as a function of these covariates. I'm not really too into the model - there are lots of cells with one relocation and I don't like the idea of creating some cell count threshold above which use is considered "significant".

I'm wondering whether there might be a smooth way to incorporate the results from an occurrence distribution into a beta distributed model (probability of use as a response to these spatial covariates) or a binomial model (pixels within 95% CI used, outside of 95% CI not used...).

I have created some test ODs for a couple of my birds and exported these as raster files using DF = "PMF" and the raster grid that my covariates are based on (100m resolution). I've pulled the ODs into QGIS and have been trying to figure out how best to use the results.

1. Does the exported OD using PMF provide an estimate of "probability of use" for each pixel? The pixel values I'm getting are TINY! Also, It doesn't seem like the exported raster is constrained to the 95% CI contour. Is there an argument I'm missing in the export function?

2. Alternatively, is there a way to export the 95% CI contour for an OD? My thinking is that pixels within the contour were "chosen" over those outside of the 95% CI.

What are your thoughts on this?

Thanks,

Teague

messages.subject_clean: Quantifying trends in resource use using occurrence distribution
messages.body_plain:
Hi Teague,

The first thing I would say with any kind of RSF model is to be careful about the autocorrelation. Almost always these models assume IID data and tracking data are usually not IID. Also, I'm not clear on why you need a cell count threshold for a Poisson point process model.

Autocorrelation aside, some kind of probabilistic interpolation could be a warranted approximation if the data are sampled irregularly in time and/or if their missingness and location error have some correspondence to the environment. Otherwise, I don't think this is a helpful step.

Off the top of my head, its not clear to me how to directly input a distribution or weighted distribution into a logistic regression. Another solution would be to first determine your effective sample size (N) and then sample N times from the occurrence distribution, or equivalently from conditional simulations. Running the analysis on the simulated samples many times would then give you an ensemble of model fits that encapsulate (to first order) the additional uncertainty and bias from the irregular sampling and location error.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: change in occurrence distribution
messages.subject_clean: change in occurrence distribution
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jenny,

I would look at how their diffusion rates change over time. The diffusion rate is the increase in area per unit time.

I haven't yet gotten around to make this convenient in the package, but if you fit a BM our IOU model, then the FIT$sigma slot is the diffusion matrix. Here's some opaque code to return diffusion rate CIs in km^2/day:

# FIT must be BM or IOU: CTMM=ctmm(range=FALSE) in ctmm.guess
diffusion <- function(FIT,level=0.95,units=TRUE)
{
  FIT$range <- TRUE
  DIFF <- ctmm:::area.covm(FIT$sigma)
  DOF <- 2*ctmm:::DOF.area(FIT)
  DIFF <- ctmm:::chisq.ci <http://chisq.ci>(DIFF,DOF=DOF,level=level)
  if(units) { DIFF <- "km^2" %#% DIFF %#% "day" } # otherwise SI units of m^2/s
  return(DIFF)
}

Note: I ran across a bug in ctmm.fit for the IOU model and the fix is now on GitHub, which you can install via devtools::install_github("ctmm-initiative/ctmm") . So please update the package first, before attempting to run this.

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris- Are there other ways to assess model fit besides the visual assessment described in the variogram vignette (https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/articles/variogram.html)? For example, there seems to be a positive relationship between the DOF[area] values and how well the model fits the variogram. Are there DOF values below which you automatically throw the model out? What about RMPSE?

Also, diving a little deeper into DOF. In the variogram vignette, it says that, "The fit parameter DOF[mean] is the number of degrees of freedom worth of data we have to estimate the stationary mean parameter, assuming that the model is correct". Could you explain why two data sets with similar number of points might have very different DOF values? I recently ran models on 50 seasonal moose home ranges and my DOF values range from 96 to 1.65 and not all of that variation can be attributed to differences in the number of observations.

Thanks!
Amanda

messages.subject_clean: Assessing model fit using DOF or RMPSE values?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Amanda,

One thing is that the variogram comparison itself can be made more exact with CI="Gauss" in variogram(), but this is very slow for large datasets (10k-100k). In principle, you can do an F-test between the empirical and theoretical variograms, but I'm not yet sure exactly how to aggregate over lags, given that the results are not independent.

If the fitted model is true, then as DOF[area] increases the variogram CIs will be tighter for more lags, and with less variability in the variograms they will match better. This can happen from effective sample size and doesn't necessarily mean that the fit is bad. For this, having the more exact CIs on the empirical variogram is good, because it doesn't assume a specific autocorrelation model.

I don't necessarily throw the model fit out based on DOF, but the default "pHREML" estimator requires a DOF of 4-5 for reasonable bias, while bootstrapping this requires a DOF of 3+. Below these values, the area estimates have a lot of negative bias. You have to ask yourself are these just crappy datasets or was the animal doing something very different like dispersing. If the datasets are of the same length, then it might be the case that the DOF=96 individuals were very range resident, while the DOF=1.96 individuals had some range shift behavior still in the data. Then if I were classifying individuals as resident or non-resident, I would probably do this based on the tau[position] parameters and not DOFs, because DOFs are sampling dependent. I'm actually working on some classification code for that at the moment. Do you think your dataset might be a good test for that?

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Maik,

Let's see... I think simplest thing to do with what you have would be to log transform the speed CIs, approximate with normal CIs, and do meta analysis on log(speed) to make them a (-Inf,Inf) random variable, rather than (0,Inf), as I'm pretty sure metafor relies on a normal assumption.

level <- 0.95 # default
alpha <- (1-level)/2 # 1-tail probability
CI <- log(CI) # log transformed CI: c(low, est, high)
PE <- CI[2] # point estimate of log(speed)
SE <- (CI[3]-CI[1]) / (qnorm(1-alpha)-qnorm(alpha)) # approximate standard error of log(speed)

This will be much easier and more exact in the next big package update.

Best,
Chris
